index.html.summary: Krafted Guards Fluent guard clauses for argument validation and precondition enforcement in .NET Krafted Guards is a .NET guard clause library with a fluent API for argument validation and precondition enforcement, making it easier to apply defensive programming and the fail-fast principle. Enforce preconditions where they apply, fail fast when a method contract is violated, and replace repetitive if/throw blocks with declarations that read like intent. Why Krafted Guards? Consider an invoice operation that requires a non-empty customer ID, an 8–30-character invoice number, at least one line, and a defined status. The examples below enforce the same preconditions and use the same exception types for corresponding failures: Manual guard clauses if (customerId == Guid.Empty) throw new ArgumentException("Customer ID cannot be empty.", nameof(customerId)); if (number is null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(number)); if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(number)) throw new ArgumentException("Invoice number cannot be empty or contain only whitespace.", nameof(number)); if (number.Length is < 8 or > 30) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(number), "Invoice number must contain between 8 and 30 characters."); if (lines is null) throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(lines)); if (lines.Count == 0) throw new ArgumentException("Invoice must contain at least one line.", nameof(lines)); if (!Enum.IsDefined(status)) throw new ArgumentException("Invoice status is not defined.", nameof(status)); Built-in .NET throw helpers if (customerId == Guid.Empty) throw new ArgumentException("Customer ID cannot be empty.", nameof(customerId)); ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(number); ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThan(number.Length, 8, nameof(number)); ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfGreaterThan(number.Length, 30, nameof(number)); ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(lines); if (lines.Count == 0) throw new ArgumentException("Invoice must contain at least one line.", nameof(lines)); if (!Enum.IsDefined(status)) throw new ArgumentException("Invoice status is not defined.", nameof(status)); Fluent guard clauses with Krafted Guards Guard.Against .Empty(customerId) .Null(number) .EmptyOrWhiteSpace(number) .Length(8, 30, number) .Null(lines) .NotAny(lines) .NotExists<InvoiceStatus>(status); Krafted Guards dramatically reduces the boilerplate required for argument validation, while reusable extensions encapsulate shared validation contracts—keeping preconditions consistent, readable, and maintainable as the codebase grows. Its core benefits include: Fluent by design — compose multiple preconditions in a single readable chain. Comprehensive validation API — validate nulls, text, collections, numbers, GUIDs, enums, predicates, regular expressions, email addresses, tax identification numbers, and other common validation scenarios. Customizable failures — override the default exception message when domain context matters. Extensible at the right scope — reuse class-specific guards locally or add reusable guard clauses through extension methods. Small binary footprint — a 28 KB assembly with no external NuGet package dependencies. Installation Install the package from NuGet: dotnet add package Krafted.Guards This package is compatible with .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10. Then import the namespace: using Krafted.Guards; Quick start Start a chain with Guard.Against and describe the conditions that make a call invalid: public class Invoice { public Invoice(Guid customerId, string billingEmail, string number, IReadOnlyCollection<InvoiceLine> lines) { Guard.Against .Empty(customerId) .Null(billingEmail) .InvalidEmail(billingEmail) .NullOrWhiteSpace(number) .Length(8, 30, number) .Null(lines) .NotAny(lines); CustomerId = customerId; BillingEmail = billingEmail; Number = number; Lines = lines; Status = InvoiceStatus.PendingApproval; } public Guid CustomerId { get; } public string BillingEmail { get; } public string Number { get; } public IReadOnlyCollection<InvoiceLine> Lines { get; } public InvoiceStatus Status { get; private set; } public decimal? ApprovedAmount { get; private set; } public string? ApprovalCode { get; private set; } public PaymentPriority? Priority { get; private set; } public void ApproveForPayment(decimal approvedAmount, string approvalCode, PaymentPriority priority) { Guard.Against .ZeroOrLess(approvedAmount) .NullOrWhiteSpace(approvalCode) .NotMatch(approvalCode, @"^APR-\d{8}$") .NotExists<PaymentPriority>(priority); ApprovedAmount = approvedAmount; ApprovalCode = approvalCode; Priority = priority; Status = InvoiceStatus.ApprovedForPayment; } // Other members omitted for brevity. } If a guard fails, it stops the chain immediately and throws a clear exception that explains the problem and identifies the invalid argument. For example, an empty customerId produces Guid cannot be empty. (Parameter 'customerId'). Each guard method validates an argument against a specific invalid condition. In this example: Empty(customerId) rejects an empty GUID. Null(billingEmail) and InvalidEmail(billingEmail) require a non-null email address and reject empty, whitespace-only, or incorrectly formatted values. NullOrWhiteSpace(number) and Length(8, 30, number) require an invoice number between 8 and 30 characters. Null(lines) and NotAny(lines) require a non-null collection containing at least one invoice line. ZeroOrLess(approvedAmount) rejects a zero or negative approved amount. NullOrWhiteSpace(approvalCode) and NotMatch(approvalCode, @"^APR-\d{8}$") require an approval code such as APR-12345678. NotExists<PaymentPriority>(priority) rejects an undefined PaymentPriority value. Custom error messages Every built-in guard accepts an optional custom message that overrides its default exception message: public void ChangePostalCode(string postalCode) { var message = $"Invalid postal code: {postalCode}."; Guard.Against .NullOrWhiteSpace(postalCode, message) .NotMatch(postalCode, @"^\d{8}$", message: message); PostalCode = postalCode; } If either guard fails, the custom message replaces its default exception message while preserving the original argument name. For example, a postalCode value of "123" produces Invalid postal code: 123. (Parameter 'postalCode'). Validating optional parameters Except for Null, NullOrEmpty, and NullOrWhiteSpace, every other built-in guard method skips validation when the value being validated is null. This allows optional parameters to be validated without explicit null checks: only non-null values are evaluated. public class Appointment { // Other members omitted for brevity. public void Reschedule(AppointmentPeriod period, string? reason = null, string? referenceCode = null) { Guard.Against .Null(period) .EmptyOrWhiteSpace(reason) .MaxLength(500, reason) .EmptyOrWhiteSpace(referenceCode) .MaxLength(50, referenceCode); Period = period; RescheduleReason = reason; ReferenceCode = referenceCode; } } In the Reschedule operation, period is required, while reason and referenceCode are optional. If an optional argument is omitted—or explicitly passed as null—the corresponding validations are skipped. When provided, reason and referenceCode cannot be empty or whitespace-only; reason cannot exceed 500 characters, and referenceCode cannot exceed 50 characters. Extensibility Krafted Guards supports two ways to reuse validation logic: 1. Reuse class-specific guards locally When a set of preconditions belongs to a single class, extract it into a local method that returns Guard. The caller can reuse the shared checks and continue the chain with operation-specific guards: public sealed class Employee { // Other members omitted for brevity. public Employee(string name, string phoneNumber, string email, EmployeeRole role, string? notes) { ThrowIfProfileInvalid(name, phoneNumber, notes) .NullOrWhiteSpace(email) .InvalidEmail(email) .NotExists<EmployeeRole>(role); // Initialize the employee... } public void UpdateProfile(string name, string phoneNumber, string? notes) { ThrowIfProfileInvalid(name, phoneNumber, notes); // Update the profile... } private static Guard ThrowIfProfileInvalid(string name, string phoneNumber, string? notes) { return Guard.Against .NullOrWhiteSpace(name) .NullOrWhiteSpace(phoneNumber) .NotMatch(phoneNumber, @"^\+?[1-9]\d{7,14}$") .EmptyOrWhiteSpace(notes); } } Here, the constructor adds email and role validations to the shared ThrowIfProfileInvalid validation method, while UpdateProfile reuses only the validations relevant to that operation. 2. Create reusable guard clause extensions When multiple guard clauses define a cohesive contract, encapsulate them in a well-named extension method on Guard. This lets callers express intent while centralizing the policy and preserving fluent chaining. Each extension should return the same Guard instance, allowing custom and built-in guard clauses to remain in the same fluent chain. The extensions below centralize an application's image-upload and resizing policies: using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis; using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; using Krafted.Guards; using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http; public static class GuardExtensions { private const long MaximumImageFileSize = 10 * 1024 * 1024; private const int MaximumImageDimension = 4096; public static Guard InvalidImageUploadRequest(this Guard guard, [NotNull] IFormFile? file, [CallerArgumentExpression("file")] string? parameterName = null) { return guard .Null(file, parameterName: parameterName) .ZeroOrLess(file.Length) .GreaterThan(MaximumImageFileSize, file.Length, message: "Image file size cannot exceed 10 MB.") .NullOrWhiteSpace(file.FileName) .MaxLength(255, file.FileName) .Match(file.FileName, @"[\\/:*?""<>|\x00-\x1F]", message: "File name contains unsupported characters.") .Match(file.FileName, @"[. ]$", message: "File name cannot end with a dot or space.") .NotMatch(file.FileName, @"\.(jpe?g|png|webp)$", message: "File name must use a supported image extension.") .NullOrWhiteSpace(file.ContentType) .NotMatch(file.ContentType, @"^image/(jpeg|png|webp)$", message: "Only JPEG, PNG, and WebP images are supported."); } public static Guard InvalidResizeOptions(this Guard guard, [NotNull] ResizeOptions? options, [CallerArgumentExpression("options")] string? parameterName = null) { return guard .Null(options, parameterName: parameterName) .ZeroOrLess(options.Width, message: "Resize width must be greater than zero.") .GreaterThan(MaximumImageDimension, options.Width, message: $"Resize width cannot exceed {MaximumImageDimension} pixels.") .ZeroOrLess(options.Height, message: "Resize height must be greater than zero.") .GreaterThan(MaximumImageDimension, options.Height, message: $"Resize height cannot exceed {MaximumImageDimension} pixels.") .LessThan(1, options.Quality, message: "Image quality must be between 1 and 100.") .GreaterThan(100, options.Quality, message: "Image quality must be between 1 and 100.") .NotExists<ResizeMode>(options.Mode, message: "Resize mode is not supported."); } } InvalidImageUploadRequest and InvalidResizeOptions are reusable and express complete contracts instead of exposing their individual validation rules. Custom guards remain chainable with built-in guards: public async Task UploadImageAsync(IFormFile file, ResizeOptions resizeOptions, ImageCategory category) { Guard.Against .InvalidImageUploadRequest(file) .InvalidResizeOptions(resizeOptions) .NotExists<ImageCategory>(category); await _imageStorage.UploadAsync(file.OpenReadStream(), file.FileName, resizeOptions, category); } Detailed policies stay cohesive and reusable while the caller remains clean and focused on the operation.
